questions.problem: Consider a linear transformation $T:{R}^{10}\to {R}^{10}.$ If $\text{rank}(T)=6$ then $\text{nullity}(T)=$
questions.worked_solution:
According to the rank-nullity theorem, if $T:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{n},$ then

$$
\text{rank}(T)+\text{nullity}(T)=n.
$$

For the given transformation, we have $n=10.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{rank}(T)+\text{nullity}(T) & =n \\ 6+\text{nullity}(T) & =10 \\ \text{nullity}(T) & =10-6 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving $-x+z=0$ for $z,$ we get $z=x.$ Therefore, any vector from $\text{Im}(T)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ x\end{aligned}]=x{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{1}}+y{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that $\text{Im}(T)=\text{Span}{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}.$ Therefore, $\text{rank}(T)=2.$ 

Finally, according the rank-nullity theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T) & =3-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =3-2 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying True Statements Using the Rank-Nullity Theorem
questions.problem:
Let $T:{R}^{5}\to {R}^{5}$ be a linear transformation whose standard matrix is $T,$ and let ${{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}}$ be a set of linearly independent vectors in ${R}^{5}.$ Consider the following statement:

*If  $\text{Im}(T)=\text{Span}{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}}$, then $\text{__________}.$ *

Which of the following can be placed into the blank space to make a true statement?

- $\text{rank}(T)=1$
- $\text{nullity}(T)=2$
- $T$ is a bijection
questions.worked_solution:
Since $T$ is a linear transformation from ${R}^{5}$ into ${R}^{5},$ the invertible matrix theorem states the following:

 $T$ is a bijection (an invertible transformation) $\,⟺\,{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Im}(T)={R}^{5} \\  & \text{rank}(T)=5 \\  & \text{Ker}(T)={0} \\  & \text{nullity}(T)=0\end{aligned}$ 

Also, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\text{rank}(T)+\text{nullity}(T)=5.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. Since $\text{Im}(T)=\text{Span}{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}}$ and the set ${{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}}$ is linearly independent, we get that $\text{rank}(T)=\text{rank}(T)=3.$

- Statement II is true. According to the rank-nullity theorem, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T) & =5-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =5-3 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $\text{rank}(T)\ne 5$ (or since $\text{nullity}(T)\ne 0$), the linear transformation $T$ cannot be a bijection according to the invertible matrix theorem.

Therefore, the correct option is "II only."

choices.value: None of the statements are true

questions.problem:
Let $T:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{n}$ be a linear transformation whose standard matrix is $T.$ Which of the following statements are true?

- If $\text{Ker}(T)={⟨x,y,z⟩\,|\,x+y=0}$ then $\text{rank}(T)+1=n$
- If there exists a vector $v\notin \text{Im}(T),$ then $|T|\ne 0$
- If ${{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}$ is linearly independent and $T({v}_{1})=T({v}_{2})=0$ then $\text{nullity}(T)=1$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $T$ is a linear transformation from ${R}^{n}$ into ${R}^{n},$ the invertible matrix theorem states the following:

 $T$ is a bijection (an invertible transformation) $\,⟺\,{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Im}(T)={R}^{n} \\  & \text{rank}(T)=n \\  & \text{Ker}(T)={0} \\  & \text{nullity}(T)=0\end{aligned}$ 

Also, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\text{rank}(T)+\text{nullity}(T)=n.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. Solving $x+y=0$ for $x,$ we get $x=-y.$ Therefore, any vector from $\text{Im}(T)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-y \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=y{{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{1}}+z{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that $\text{Ker}(T)=\text{Span}{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}.$ Therefore, $\text{nullity}(T)=2.$ Finally, according the rank-nullity theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{rank}(T)+\text{nullity}(T) & =n \\ \text{rank}(T)+2 & =n.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. If $v\notin \text{Im}(T)$ then $\text{Im}(T)\ne {R}^{n}$, so, according to the invertible matrix theorem, $T$ is not a bijection. Thus, the matrix $T$ is not invertible, and, consequently, $|T|=0.$

- Statement III is false. Since $T({v}_{1})=T({v}_{2})=0$, then ${v}_{1},{v}_{2}\in \text{Ker}(T).$ But the vectors are linearly independent, therefore, the dimension of  $\text{Ker}(T)$ is at least $2.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true."

questions.problem:
Let $T:{R}^{3}\to {R}^{3}$ be a linear transformation whose standard matrix is $T.$ Which of the following statements are true?

- If $\text{Im}(T)={[x,y,z]^{T}\,:\,x=0}$ then $\text{nullity}(T)=1$
- If $\text{Ker}(T)={[x,y,z]^{T}\,:\,y-2z=0,x+z=0}$ then $\text{rank}(T)=2$
- If ${v}_{1},$ ${v}_{2},$ and ${v}_{3}$ are the columns of $T$ and ${v}_{3}={v}_{1}-{v}_{2}$, then $\text{Ker}(T)\ne {0}$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $T$ is a linear transformation from ${R}^{3}$ into ${R}^{3},$ the invertible matrix theorem states the following:

 $T$ is a bijection (an invertible transformation) $\,⟺\,{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Im}(T)={R}^{3} \\  & \text{rank}(T)=3 \\  & \text{Ker}(T)={0} \\  & \text{nullity}(T)=0\end{aligned}$ 

Also, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\text{rank}(T)+\text{nullity}(T)=3.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. Any vector from $\text{Im}(T)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=y{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{1}}+z{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that $\text{Im}(T)=\text{Span}{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}.$ Therefore, $\text{rank}(T)=2.$ Finally, according the rank-nullity theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T) & =3-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =3-2 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Solving $y-2z=0$ for $y,$ we get $y=2z.$ Solving $x+z=0$ for $x,$ we get $x=-z.$ Therefore, any vector from $\text{Im}(T)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-z \\ 2z \\ z\end{aligned}]=z{{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that $\text{Ker}(T)=\text{Span}{{v}_{1}}.$ Therefore, $\text{nullity}(T)=1.$ Finally, according the rank-nullity theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{rank}(T) & =3-\text{nullity}(T) \\  & =3-1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. If the columns of $T$ are such that ${v}_{3}={v}_{1}-{v}_{2},$ then the set of vectors ${{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}}$ is linearly dependent and therefore $\text{Im}(T)=\text{Col}(T)\ne {R}^{3}.$ Now, according to the matrix invertible theorem, we obtain that $\text{Ker}(T)\ne {0}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

- If $[-2,0,0]^{T}$ is a solution of $T(x)=0$ then $\text{nullity}(T)\ne 0$
- If $T(x)=[1,0,0]^{T}$ has no solution then $\text{rank}(T)=3$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $T$ is a linear transformation from ${R}^{3}$ into ${R}^{3},$ the invertible matrix theorem states the following:

 $T$ is a bijection (an invertible transformation) $\,⟺\,{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Im}(T)={R}^{3} \\  & \text{rank}(T)=3 \\  & \text{Ker}(T)={0} \\  & \text{nullity}(T)=0\end{aligned}$ 

Also, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\text{rank}(T)+\text{nullity}(T)=3.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. According to the rank-nullity theorem, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T) & =3-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =3-2 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{Ker}(T)\ne {0}.$

- Statement II is true. Since $[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ is a solution of $Tx=0$, we have that $[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\in \text{Ker}(T)$ and therefore $\text{nullity}(T)\ne 0.$

- Statement III is false. Since $T(x)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ has no solution, we have that $\text{Im}(T)\ne {R}^{3}.$ Hence, $\text{rank}(T)\ne 3.$

Therefore, the correct option is "II only."

canonical_examples.problem: Consider a linear transformation $\mathbf{T}:\mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^3.$ If $\textrm{nullity}(\mathbf{T})=1,$ then what is $\textrm{rank}(\mathbf{T})?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
According to the rank-nullity theorem, if $\mathbf{T}:\mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n,$ then

$$
\textrm{rank}(\mathbf{T}) + \textrm{nullity}(\mathbf{T}) = n.
$$

For the given transformation, we have $n=3.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{rank}(T)+\text{nullity}(T) & =n \\ \text{rank}(T)+1 & =3 \\ \text{rank}(T) & =3-1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$
